doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Active listening and jazz history teaching
summary: Active listening, Masso's late discovery of Armstrong, and the need for required listening lists.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It was his personality. If you were to design a course, a jazz history course, would there be things that you would emphasize? You mentioned active listening. Maybe that’s more my question. What does active listening mean to you?

Well I guess it means listening and making judgments as you go along on what you like — say oh listen to that chorus, listen to what Lester does in this particular phrase, or gee, I don’t know why so and so did that. Listening to the music for what’s inside of it. As far as jazz history, I really don’t feel competent to be able to get into that because I’m as guilty as a lot of other musicians in that when I started to play, that’s where I started to listen. I didn’t go back. I didn’t listen to Louis Armstrong until years later. And I should
have when I first started to play. He had so much to say and so many of those player, Bix Beiderbecke and players in the early twenties.

I think that’s usually the case, and then sometimes hopefully people’s tastes will, or at least their listening habits will work backwards to see what went on before. And of course now with the young players, they’re starting with Kenny G and Grover Washington and those kind of players, and getting their jazz from that. They have a lot farther to work backwards I guess.

They do. And I certainly hope that somebody will make it imperative that they do it. But you know people who are designing these History of Jazz classes really should have a listening list and a required listening list, and demand some feedback from the listening.
